title: Midterm Exam Reviewer
description: Chapters 5–8: Database Query Languages, Data Organization and Architecture, Data Governance, and Special Purpose Databases.

notes.heading: Ch. 5 · What a Query Language Is
notes.summary: A query language is a specialized computer language used to make queries and retrieve information from databases. It serves as the interface between users and the database management system (DBMS). A query is simply a request for data or information from a database, written in a language the database understands.
points: Queries can find, summarize, filter, combine, adjust, delete, insert, and update data
Basic types of queries - select, parameter, make-table, append, and crosstab queries
SQL (Structured Query Language) is the most popular query language for relational databases

notes.heading: Ch. 5 · Two Types of Query Languages
notes.summary: SQL is declarative because it describes what needs to be accomplished rather than how, but it also includes some procedural elements.

manages transactions to keep data consistent - COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT

uses key values, graphs, wide columns, and documents; dynamic schemas for unstructured data and big data

notes.heading: Ch. 5 · Query Languages vs. Programming Languages
points: Programming languages (Python, Java) build software applications
Query languages are specialized for interacting with databases and do not compile software
Query commands are concise, so one statement can replace many lines of program code

notes.heading: Ch. 5 · Use Cases and Applications
points: Extracting relevant data - get specific data quickly without manual extraction
Filtering, sorting, and updating data without editing each record by hand
Aggregating data - SUM, COUNT, AVERAGE, MAX
Managing data integrity - ACID properties in SQL
Applied in web development, Business Intelligence (BI), data warehousing, and database administration

notes.heading: Ch. 6 · Data Architecture
notes.summary: Data architecture describes how data is managed from collection through transformation, distribution, and consumption. It is the blueprint for how data flows through storage systems, and its design should be driven by business requirements.
points: A good data architecture keeps data manageable and useful, supports data lifecycle management, avoids redundant storage, improves data quality, and enables new applications
Data lifecycle management - managing data from the moment it is created and stored until it is archived or destroyed
Modern data architectures often leverage cloud platforms

notes.heading: Ch. 6 · Three Types of Data Models

terms.definition: big-picture view of what the system contains, how it is organized, and the business rules; made while gathering initial requirements
more detail - data types, lengths, and relationships among entities; no technical system requirements
most detailed - actual implementation such as table structures, indexes, and storage; used for schema creation and optimization

notes.heading: Ch. 6 · Data Architecture Frameworks (IBM standard)
points: TOGAF's 4 pillars - Business Architecture (structure, strategy, processes), Data Architecture (data assets and their lifecycle), Application Architecture (application systems and how they relate), Technical Architecture (hardware, software, networking)

notes.heading: Ch. 6 · Types of Data Architecture
points: Benefits of data architecture - reducing redundancy, improving data quality, enabling integration, and data lifecycle management

notes.heading: Ch. 6 · Data Organization
notes.summary: Data organization is arranging information through sorting, storing, and finding data so you can work smarter and make better decisions. Raw data is hard to analyze, so it must be organized first.
points: Why organize - Enhanced Decision-Making, Improved Productivity, Data Accuracy and Consistency, Scalability and Growth
Ways to organize - Folder Structures, Database Management, Data Classification (by importance or sensitivity), Automation Tools, and CRM such as HubSpot

notes.heading: Ch. 7 · What Data Governance Is
notes.summary: Data Governance (DG) is the exercise of authority and control (planning, monitoring, and enforcement) over the management of data assets. Its purpose is to make sure data is managed properly, according to policies and best practices. DG focuses on how decisions about data are made and how people and processes should behave toward data.
points: Like an auditor, DG oversees data management without directly executing it - a separation of duty between oversight and execution
Most DG programs include - Strategy, Policy, Standards and quality, Oversight (stewardship), Compliance, Issue management, Data management projects, and Data asset valuation

terms.definition: general risk management (finances, reputation, E-Discovery), data security, and privacy of PII
regulatory compliance, data quality improvement, Metadata Management (business glossary), efficiency in development projects (SDLC), and vendor management (data contracts)

notes.heading: Ch. 7 · Goals and Principles
notes.summary: The goal of DG is to enable an organization to manage data as an asset.
points: Principles - Leadership and strategy, Business-driven, Shared responsibility (business data stewards and technical professionals), Multi-layered (enterprise and local levels), Framework-based, and Principle-based

notes.heading: Ch. 7 · Data Stewardship
notes.summary: Data Stewardship is the most common label for accountability and responsibility for data. A steward manages the property of another person; custodian and trustee are synonyms.
points: Activities - creating and managing core Metadata (Business Glossary), documenting rules and standards, managing data quality issues, and executing operational DG activities
Types - Chief, Executive, Enterprise, Business, Data Owner, Technical, and Coordinating Data Stewards

notes.heading: Ch. 7 · Data Policies and Data Asset Valuation
points: Ways to measure value - Replacement cost (data lost in a disaster or breach), Market value (merger or acquisition), Identified opportunities (income from insights), Selling data, and Risk cost (penalties, remediation, litigation)

notes.heading: Ch. 8 · Special Purpose Databases
notes.summary: Special purpose databases are tailored for specific use cases - for example multimedia databases for images and video, in-memory databases for faster access, and distributed databases for fault tolerance across multiple nodes.

notes.heading: Ch. 8 · Trends in Modern Databases
notes.summary: "Data is the new oil." Organizations store more data than ever, so they need secure, high-performing ways to store and use large, diverse data sets while keeping quality, accuracy, and integrity.

Type of data analytics that focuses on discovering and explaining data characteristics and relationships based on existing data.
Type of data analytics that focuses on predicting future data outcomes with a high degree of accuracy.
Uncovers hidden trends, patterns, and relationships in vast datasets, forming computer models to explain findings and support decision-making.
questions.explanation: Chapter 8 - Special Purpose Databases. It focuses on the discovery and explanation stages in knowledge acquisition.
